sections.title: 3 Threat Model
sections.text: 3 Threat Model 3.1 Trusted Model The MCP workflow consists of three primary parties (as shown in Figure 1 ): the users, the MCP Host, and the MCP Servers. The Users. The users are assumed to be honest and non-colluding. They issue benign queries to the agent via the Host, from which they receive the final responses. MCP Host. The MCP Host is assumed to be trusted and serves as the application environment that contains the LLM agent and the client that manages communication. Given a user query and the system prompt, the Host orchestrates tool invocations and returns a final response to the user based on the tool execution results. MCP Servers. The MCP Servers are treated as untrusted components. When the MCP Host concurrently connects to a benign server [LaTeX: A] A A (with a legitimate tool set [LaTeX: \mathcal{T}_{A}] 𝒯 A \mathcal{T}_{A} ) and an attacker-controlled server [LaTeX: B] B B (exposing a poisoned tool [LaTeX: T_{K}] T K T_{K} ), the poisoned tool is loaded into the agent’s system prompt alongside the benign tools. This enables the adversary to manipulate the agent’s tool invocation through the attack payload of [LaTeX: T_{K}] T K T_{K} , thereby inducing malicious operations. 3.2 Attacker’s Capabilities We consider a black-box setting where the attacker lacks access to the users’ actual queries and the internal parameters of the LLM agent hosted by the MCP Host. However, the attacker can inspect the toolset [LaTeX: \mathcal{T}_{A}] 𝒯 A \mathcal{T}_{A} exposed by benign server [LaTeX: A] A A to select an original tool [LaTeX: T_{A}] T A T_{A} and a high-privilege target tool [LaTeX: T_{G}] T G T_{G} . In addition, the attacker can craft the poisoned tool [LaTeX: T_{K}] T K T_{K} and propagate it to public marketplaces via an attacker-controlled MCP server. 3.3 Attacker’s Goals The attacker’s primary objective is to execute successful implicit tool poisoning attacks. For any user query that would otherwise trigger the invocation of [LaTeX: T_{A}] T A T_{A} , the attacker aims to subvert the agent’s decision, redirecting it to invoke a legitimate but high-privilege tool [LaTeX: T_{G}\in\mathcal{T}_{A},\;T_{G}\neq T_{A}] T G ∈ 𝒯 A , T G ≠ T A T_{G}\in\mathcal{T}_{A},\;T_{G}\neq T_{A} to perform malicious operations, while ensuring that the poisoned tool [LaTeX: T_{K}] T K T_{K} remains dormant and is never directly executed throughout the attack process. Furthermore, the attacker seeks to maintain evasiveness, ensuring that the poisoned tool circumvents existing malicious tool detection mechanisms.

sections.text: 4 Methodology 4.1 System Overview MCP-ITP provides an automated framework that crafts tools for implicit tool poisoning attacks. As shown in Figure 2 , it consists of three key components: an attacker LLM [LaTeX: L_{A}] L A L_{A} that iteratively optimizes poisoned tools, a malicious tool detector LLM [LaTeX: L_{D}] L D L_{D} , and an effectiveness evaluator LLM [LaTeX: L_{E}] L E L_{E} . Given the legitimate tool set [LaTeX: \mathcal{T}_{A}] 𝒯 A \mathcal{T}_{A} exposed by target MCP server [LaTeX: A] A A , we first select an original tool [LaTeX: T_{A}] T A T_{A} and a target tool [LaTeX: T_{G}] T G T_{G} . The attacker LLM [LaTeX: L_{A}] L A L_{A} then generates a sequence of candidate poisoned tools using an iterative optimization strategy, and submits each candidate to [LaTeX: L_{D}] L D L_{D} and [LaTeX: L_{E}] L E L_{E} for assessment. The outputs from [LaTeX: L_{D}] L D L_{D} and [LaTeX: L_{E}] L E L_{E} are aggregated as feedback and passed to subsequent iterations to guide [LaTeX: L_{A}] L A L_{A} in refining the candidate poisoned tools. The optimization process terminates when either a predefined effectiveness criterion is satisfied or a maximum number of iterations is reached, at which point the best-performing candidate is selected as the final poisoned tool [LaTeX: T_{K}] T K T_{K} . 4.2 Constructing [LaTeX: R] R R for Relevance We decompose the poisoned tool description [LaTeX: \mathrm{desc}(T_{K})] desc ⁡ ( T K ) \mathrm{desc}(T_{K}) into two distinct subsequences, [LaTeX: R] R R and [LaTeX: S] S S , where [LaTeX: R] R R is crafted to maximize semantic alignment with [LaTeX: \mathrm{desc}(T_{A})] desc ⁡ ( T A ) \mathrm{desc}(T_{A}) and [LaTeX: S] S S realizes the implicit poisoning functionality. sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.text: 5 Experiments 5.1 Experiment Settings LLM Agents. We instantiate MCP-ITP with DeepSeek-V3 as the attacker model [LaTeX: L_{A}] L A L_{A} , Qwen3-32b as the evaluator model [LaTeX: L_{E}] L E L_{E} , and Qwen3-8b as the detector model [LaTeX: L_{D}] L D L_{D} . We evaluate MCP-ITP across 12 prominent LLM agents, including models from GPT [ 35 ] , DeepSeek [ 36 ] , Qwen [ 37 ] , and Gemini [ 38 ] . For Qwen3, which supports toggling its reasoning mode on and off, we evaluate both with reasoning enabled and disabled to analyze its impact on attack success rates. Dataset. We conduct experiments on MCPTox dataset. MCPTox is built on 45 real-world running MCP servers and 353 real tools, and contains a total of 1,497 malicious test cases. We focus on the subset of test cases corresponding to implicit poisoning paradigms (548 cases) and compare MCP-ITP against the hand-crafted poisoned tools in MCPTox under the same server/tool contexts and queries. MCP Implementation. We implement our MCP pipeline based on the open-source MCP codebase [ 39 ] and adopt its default system prompt. Evaluation Metrics. Our primary metrics are the Attack Success Rate (ASR) and the Malicious Tool Detection Rate (MDR). ASR measures the vulnerability of an agent to implicit tool poisoning and is computed as the number of successful attacks ( [LaTeX: N_{sa}] N s ​ a N_{sa} ) divided by the total number of valid agent responses ( [LaTeX: N_{vr}] N v ​ r N_{vr} ), excluding invalid generations, i.e., [LaTeX: ASR=\frac{N_{sa}}{N_{vr}}] A ​ S ​ R = N s ​ a N v ​ r ASR=\frac{N_{sa}}{N_{vr}} . MDR measures the evasiveness of the poisoned tool against malicious tool detection methods and is calculated as the number of times that the poisoning tool is flagged as malicious ( [LaTeX: N_{m}] N m N_{m} ) divided by the total number of valid outputs ( [LaTeX: N_{v}] N v N_{v} ), i.e., [LaTeX: MDR=\frac{N_{m}}{N_{v}}] M ​ D ​ R = N m N v MDR=\frac{N_{m}}{N_{v}} . Optimization Hyperparameters. Unless otherwise stated, we use the default hyperparameters (Algorithm 1 ): the number of candidates [LaTeX: N=5] N = 5 N=5 , tree width [LaTeX: W=1] W = 1 W=1 , and the number of iterations [LaTeX: T=3] T = 3 T=3 . Evaluation Metrics. To comprehensively assess the performance of MCP-ITP, we employ two primary metrics: (i) Attack Success Rate (ASR), which quantifies the effectiveness of the implicit tool poisoning. It is defined as the ratio of successful attacks ( [LaTeX: N_{sa}] N s ​ a N_{sa} ) to the total number of valid agent responses ( [LaTeX: N_{vr}] N v ​ r N_{vr} ), excluding failed or irrelevant generations: [LaTeX: ASR=\frac{N_{sa}}{N_{vr}}] A ​ S ​ R = N s ​ a N v ​ r ASR=\frac{N_{sa}}{N_{vr}} . (ii) Malicious Tool Detection Rate (MDR), which evaluates the stealthiness of the poisoned tool against detection mechanisms. It is defined as the ratio of the number of instances where the poisoned tool is flagged as malicious ( [LaTeX: N_{m}] N m N_{m} ) over the total number of valid outputs ( [LaTeX: N_{v}] N v N_{v} ): [LaTeX: MDR=\frac{N_{m}}{N_{v}}] M ​ D ​ R = N m N v MDR=\frac{N_{m}}{N_{v}} . 5.2 Main Results Our approach achieves high ASR and low MDR. Table 1 reports the ASR of MCP-ITP across 12 LLM agent settings, together with a breakdown of failure modes. We run a single evaluation per setting. Here, Ignored refers to instances where the agent remains unaffected by poisoning and falls back to the original tool [LaTeX: T_{A}] T A T_{A} . Direct refers to directly invoking the poisoned tool [LaTeX: T_{K}] T K T_{K} . Others covers invoking other tools or refusing to respond. In general, MCP-ITP achieves high ASR across a range of LLM agents, e.g., 82.9% on o1-mini, 78.4% on DeepSeek-V3, and 84.2% on GPT-3.5-turbo. Figure 4(c) further shows that additional optimization iterations increase ASR across models, suggesting that iterative optimization can progressively refine poisoned tools and improve attack effectiveness. Most failures arise from Ignored behavior. In contrast, Direct or Others are relatively more frequent for certain models, indicating model-dependent differences in tool-selection policy and instruction adherence. Meanwhile, Figure 4 shows low MDR for MCP-ITP under different detection methods. Under AI-Infra-Guard, MDR is 0.3% on Qwen3-14b and 1.0% on o1-mini; under Oracle, MDR is 22.0% and 31.4%, respectively. These results indicate that the implicitly poisoned tools generated by MCP-ITP achieve high attack effectiveness while maintaining evasiveness. (a) HyperBrowser (b) Memory (c) Email (d) Github Figure 3 : Detail results across different MCP Servers. (a) AI-Infra-Guard (b) Oracle Figure 4 : MDR results of MCP-ITP and MCPTox under different settings. Our approach outperforms the baseline. Compared with manually crafted poisoned tools in MCPTox, MCP-ITP achieves higher ASR across 12 LLM agent settings. For example, ASR increases from 48.2% to 84.2% on GPT-3.5-turbo, from 44.8% to 78.4% on DeepSeek-V3, and from 45.1% to 69.9% on Qwen3-32b + . Overall, 8/12 settings improve by over 10 percentage points. Analyzing the failure-type distribution, we find that the ASR gains are primarily driven by fewer Ignored cases. On o1-mini, Ignored drops from 19.9% to 4.2%, and on DeepSeek-V3 from 38.0% to 14.8%. This indicates that, relative to the baseline, MCP-ITP increases the likelihood of invoking the targeted tool [LaTeX: T_{G}] T G T_{G} over the original tool [LaTeX: T_{A}] T A T_{A} . Beyond ASR, MCP-ITP also exhibits improved evasiveness. Figure 4 shows that MCP-ITP attains lower MDR than MCPTox under both detection methods (AI-Infra-Guard and Oracle) [ 12 , 40 ] . For o1-mini, MDR drops from 17.22% to 0.96% under AI-Infra-Guard and from 77.35% to 31.39% under Oracle. In general, these results suggest that MCP-ITP more reliably manipulates agents to deviate from [LaTeX: T_{A}] T A T_{A} and invoke the target tool [LaTeX: T_{G}] T G T_{G} in a real MCP environment, while remaining less detectable by existing mechanisms. As shown in Figure 4(d) , Qwen3 models show a pronounced trend of increasing vulnerability with the model capability under MCP-ITP. Under the same evaluation settings, Qwen3-32b achieves higher ASR than Qwen3-8b, and o1-mini further exceeds Qwen3-32b. Moreover, enabling reasoning mode substantially increases ASR: Qwen3-8b rises from 7.44% to 40.5%, and Qwen3-32b from 28.8% to 69.9%. sections.title: Limitations
sections.text: Limitations In this paper, we propose MCP-ITP, which uses an iterative optimization strategy to craft tools for implicit tool poisoning attacks in MCP settings. When stronger models are employed by LLM-based malicious tool detection methods, the MDR of MCP-ITP still increases. Designing poisoned tools that better evade such detection mechanisms without significantly compromising attack effectiveness remains an important direction for future research. In addition, our experimental evaluation is currently restricted to the MCPTox dataset for MCP tool poisoning, primarily because the available datasets for MCP-specific implicit tool poisoning are still limited. Future work should extend the evaluation to newly developed or broader datasets to enable a more comprehensive and comparative assessment of MCP-ITP. Finally, we focus on extensive empirical evaluation to demonstrate MCP-ITP’s attack effectiveness and evasiveness, rather than providing a formal theoretical analysis.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.text: Ethical Considerations This research aims to responsibly identify vulnerabilities in LLM through implicit tool poisoning attacks. Our sole intent is to raise security awareness and encourage the development of stronger defences, not to enable harmful misuse. We acknowledge that the techniques explored in this work could be misused if applied irresponsibly. To mitigate this risk, we did not deploy these attacks in real-world settings or against live systems. All experiments were conducted in controlled environments to avoid causing real-world harm. By communicating these risks, we hope this work promotes the development of more robust, ethical, and reliable AI technologies. We do not collect, process, or store real personal data. The dataset used in our experiments is open and transparent, and any PII is randomly generated, ensuring no real individuals’ privacy is compromised. We emphasize that advancements in adversarial understanding should always be accompanied by proactive defense strategies to ensure the safe and responsible deployment of AI technologies.
